title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Definitions: Which of these best defines the control flow of an LLM system?

options.text: The data each step passes to the next step, such as the model's text or a tool result
The decision of which step runs next, and when the whole process stops
The set of tools, and their descriptions, that the model may call during one request
The prompt that tells the model how to behave at each step

items.stem: Definitions: Which of these best defines a workflow, as opposed to an agent?

options.text: A system that calls the model once per request and returns its reply as is
A system that makes more than one model call to finish a request
A system where the developer's program, not the model, picks each step
A system where the model only writes text and never calls any tool

items.stem: Definitions: In one phrase, what is an agent, as opposed to a workflow?
Definitions: In a few words, name two things that typically get worse when the model, rather than code, owns the control flow.
Definitions: In one phrase, what do you give up when you choose a fixed workflow instead of an agent?

Applying it: A teammate proposes this makerspace design. Python calls check_training_record(student_id) on every request. If it returns False, the program prints "Complete training first" and ends. If it returns True, the program passes the student's message to a model together with the three tools search_manual, get_slots and book_slot. The model may call any of them, in any order, as many times as it likes, and its final text is shown to the student. Who owns the control flow?

options.text: Code owns the check and the early stop; the model owns the flow after that
Code owns the check and the early stop; code also owns the order of search_manual, get_slots and book_slot after that
The model owns the whole flow, including whether training is checked, because it receives the student's message
Code owns the whole flow, because code runs both the check and the call to the model

items.stem: Applying it: A request goes through three stages. Stage 1: the model returns JSON naming the machine and date from the student's message. Stage 2: a line of Python passes that machine name to get_slots. Stage 3: the model writes the reply from the returned slots. A teammate says this is an agent because the model is called twice. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is an agent, because the model's summary decides which tool call comes next
It is a workflow: the model never chooses what runs next; it only writes text and JSON
It is an agent, because the model is called twice and a workflow would call it only once
It is neither, because a system needs tools to count as either

items.stem: Applying it: Every booking request runs the same two availability checks and then book_slot, in that order, and nothing in a request changes that (book_slot is a plain function call, not a model call). Design A is code that calls the model for each of 3 steps (calendar summary, training summary, booking confirmation). Design B is an agent that, averaged over past requests, makes 6 model calls. Each model call costs $0.005, and the makerspace expects 2,000 booking requests per month. What is the monthly model cost, in dollars, of the design that fits this request type?

Applying it: A teammate wants the manual question-answering path to be an agent. The logs of 500 past questions show the same sequence every time: one search_manual call, then one model call that writes the answer from the passages. The team has a small model budget. Which response is strongest?

options.text: Use an agent: it can recover when a step fails, and that reliability is worth its higher cost on the busiest path of the whole assistant
Use an agent: the model finds better passages when it chooses its own searches
Keep a fixed workflow, but add a loop so the model can search again if the first passages look weak
Keep a fixed workflow: the logged path never varied, so an agent's extra calls would add cost with no decision for it to make

items.stem: Applying it: Compare two student requests. Request X: "Is the laser cutter free Friday afternoon?" Request Y: "Is the laser cutter free Friday afternoon? If not, find the soonest slot on any machine I am trained on that can cut 3 mm acrylic." Which request could code own end to end, which needs the model to own the control flow after the first lookup, and what property of the requests separates them?
